source.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019

observed_symptoms.fact: A WAF Managed Rules change was deployed automatically; three minutes later the first PagerDuty page fired from a synthetic WAF test, followed by other end-to-end test failures, a global traffic drop alert, widespread 502s and PoP reports of CPU exhaustion.
CPUs handling HTTP/HTTPS traffic spiked to nearly 100% on every core worldwide; customers saw 502 pages on any Cloudflare domain.
A Solutions Engineering leader reported about 80% of traffic lost during the incident.
Outage lasted 27 minutes; traffic and CPU returned to normal at 14:09 after global WAF termination at 14:07; WAF re-enabled globally at 14:52.

Core proxying, CDN and WAF functionality went down; Cloudflare's other protection mechanisms kept operating. Internal tools and customer dashboard/API were also hindered because they run through the edge.

confirmed_root_cause.mechanism: A new XSS-detection WAF rule contained a regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU on all HTTP/HTTPS-serving cores. The rule was pushed globally in seconds through Quicksilver, even though it was deployed in simulate mode, because rules must still execute to be evaluated.
confirmed_elements: Single WAF rule with catastrophic-backtracking regex
WAF used PCRE inside Lua, a backtracking engine with no complexity guarantees
A CPU-use protection had been removed by mistake in an earlier refactor
Tests did not detect runaway CPU; SOP allowed global rule push without staging
contributing_factors: Rollback plan required running the full WAF build twice
Access outage blocked authentication to internal tools; a rarely used bypass was needed
Some engineers' credentials had been disabled for inactivity
Status page and first traffic-drop alert were slow

investigation_evidence.evidence: Synthetic WAF test paged first, followed by many end-to-end failures and PoP CPU exhaustion reports.
Performance Team pulled live CPU data from a machine showing the WAF was responsible.
Another engineer confirmed with strace; error logs also showed the WAF in trouble.
An attack was dismissed as the cause once the WAF was identified.
Log files from previous WAF builds showed no increase in test-suite run time for the offending rule.
In a single city, using a subset of traffic after removing paying customers, engineers ran negative tests (was this change the cause) and positive tests (did the rollback work).

recovery_actions.action: Executed a global terminate that disabled the WAF worldwide.
recovery_actions.why: Fastest way to stop CPU exhaustion; the rest of Cloudflare's protections continued.

recovery_actions.action: Rolled back the offending rule change and re-enabled the WAF globally after single-city tests.

recovery_verification.method: Traffic levels and CPU returned to expected worldwide after the global terminate.
Negative and positive tests in one isolated city; team was 100% satisfied before global re-enable.

acceptable_alternatives.description: Global WAF terminate as an immediate mitigation
acceptable_alternatives.basis: R1; removes WAF protection globally while active

acceptable_alternatives.description: Re-introduce the removed CPU protection; switch to re2 or Rust regex engines; add rule profiling to tests
acceptable_alternatives.basis: Post-incident remediation list; engine switch had an ETA of July 31 and was not used to recover

not_stated_in_source: That DNS remained available during the incident (the post does not say so)
Any repair cost or relative effort

fixture_alignment.hypothesis_alignment: H02 is correct; source adds contributing causes (removed CPU protection, no staged rollout).

A01.note: Disabling CDN caching is not in the source and does not address CPU exhaustion.

A02.note: Rule rollback; note the very first mitigation was a global WAF terminate, not a rollback.

A03.note: A safer regex engine was a follow-up, not a recovery action.

A04.note: Both components are individually source-stated but never as one recovery action; the cost is a fixture invention.
